oneLineAnswer: A prescription ointment that blocks PDE-4 in the skin, approved for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis (eczema).
whatItIs: Crisaborole is the active ingredient in a prescription skin ointment. In the United States it is sold as Eucrisa, and generic versions exist. It is a phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE-4) inhibitor, which means it blocks an enzyme called phosphodiesterase 4. The ointment contains 20 mg of crisaborole per gram, or 2%. The FDA first approved it in 2016.
whatItDoes: Crisaborole treats mild to moderate atopic dermatitis, the itchy skin condition most people call eczema.
It belongs to a drug class called phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE-4) inhibitors, which block that enzyme.
Blocking PDE-4 raises levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) inside cells, the label explains.
In two 28-day trials, 32.8% and 31.4% of crisaborole users reached clear or almost clear skin.
Vehicle users in those same trials scored 25.4% and 18.0% on the same measure.
howPeopleUseIt: It is a prescription ointment you apply to affected skin, not a pill or an over-the-counter cream.
The label describes a thin layer applied twice daily to affected areas.
Once clinical effect appears, the label says reducing to once daily may be considered.
The label states it is for topical use only, not for the eyes, mouth, or vagina.
A 52-week trial also studied once-daily use in people who first improved on twice-daily use.

commonSideEffects: Application site pain was the most common reaction in the trials.
The label explains this covers skin sensations such as burning or stinging.
About 4% of crisaborole users reported it, against about 1% of vehicle users.
Contact urticaria (hives) occurred in fewer than 1% of treated subjects.
seriousSigns: Hypersensitivity reactions, including contact urticaria, have occurred with crisaborole, the label says.
The label names severe itching, swelling, and redness at the application site or elsewhere.
Allergic contact dermatitis has been reported after approval through voluntary reports, the label notes.
whoShouldAvoid: The label lists known hypersensitivity to crisaborole or any ingredient of the ointment as a contraindication.
Safety and effectiveness below 3 months of age have not been established.

interactions: Crisaborole and one of its metabolites are not expected to inhibit several cytochrome P450 enzymes under clinical conditions.
Lab tests found a second metabolite weakly inhibited CYP1A2 and CYP2B6 and moderately inhibited CYP2C8 and CYP2C9.
A clinical trial using warfarin, which CYP2C9 processes, showed no drug interaction potential, the label says.
pregnancyAndChildren: Human pregnancy data come only from case reports, which the label calls insufficient to judge risk. Animal studies found no fetal harm at 3 times the human dose in rats and 2 times in rabbits. No one knows whether crisaborole passes into human milk, and the label notes the drug is absorbed systemically. In children, safety and effectiveness are established from 3 months of age and older. Clinical studies did not include enough people aged 65 and over to show a different response.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The label says the exact way crisaborole helps atopic dermatitis is not well defined.
Whether crisaborole reaches breast milk, or affects a breastfed baby, is unknown.
Human data in pregnancy are too thin to estimate risk of birth defects or miscarriage.
Effects in people aged 65 and older are not well described, because the studies enrolled too few.
Efficacy data in the label rest on 28-day and 52-week periods, so longer use is not described.
The label reports no head-to-head comparison against other prescription eczema treatments.

evidence.claim: Crisaborole ointment is approved for topical treatment of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis from 3 months of age.
evidence.quote: EUCRISA is indicated for topical treatment of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in adult and pediatric patients 3 months of age and older.

evidence.claim: Crisaborole is a PDE-4 inhibitor and raises cAMP inside cells.
evidence.quote: Crisaborole is a phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE-4) inhibitor. PDE-4 inhibition results in increased intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels.

evidence.claim: Application site pain is the most common adverse reaction.
evidence.quote: The most common adverse reaction occurring in ≥1% in subjects is application site pain.

evidence.claim: Hypersensitivity may show as severe itching, swelling, and redness at the application site or elsewhere.
evidence.quote: Hypersensitivity should be suspected in the event of severe pruritus, swelling and erythema at the application site or at a distant site.

evidence.claim: Two vehicle-controlled trials randomized subjects 2:1 to crisaborole or vehicle twice daily for 28 days.
evidence.quote: subjects were randomized 2:1 to receive EUCRISA or vehicle applied twice daily for 28 days

evidence.claim: Trial success rates were 32.8% and 31.4% for crisaborole against 25.4% and 18.0% for vehicle.
Known hypersensitivity to crisaborole or any ingredient is a contraindication.
evidence.quote: EUCRISA is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to crisaborole or any component of the formulation.

evidence.claim: The 2% strength is 20 mg of crisaborole per gram of ointment.
evidence.quote: Ointment: 20 mg of crisaborole per gram (2%) of white to off-white ointment.

evidence.claim: PubChem records crisaborole as CID 44591583, formula C14H10BNO3, with a benzoxaborole structure.
Atopic dermatitis is the most common form of eczema and affects babies and children most often.
evidence.quote: The most common type of eczema is atopic dermatitis. It is most common in babies and children, but adults can have it too.

gaps: NCCIH has no crisaborole page and its eczema page also returned 404, so no NCCIH content is cited.
LiverTox returned no crisaborole entry, so liver-specific information is not covered.
DailyMed's drugInfo.cfm view served a JavaScript shell with no readable text; the label was read from the DailyMed fdaDrugXsl.cfm render instead.
The openFDA record holds a single label document, so openFDA and DailyMed evidence traces back to the same prescribing information.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded by instruction because NLM licenses them from a copyrighted publisher.
No dose or personal-use guidance is given here by design; only what the label records is reported, attributed.
ClinicalTrials.gov records confirm registered crisaborole studies exist but no trial result detail was used as a claim.
summary: This record covers what crisaborole is, the skin condition the label approves it for, and what the label reports about side effects, warnings, interactions, and gaps.
